title: Pay the exact amount
goal: I can count coins and notes and pay an exact amount. I can find all the ways and the fewest coins.

learn.intro: Our coins are 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ and 50¢. A $1 coin is worth 100¢. Notes ($2, $5, $10) are worth more. To pay an amount, start with the largest coin that fits. To find every way, list them in a table.

example.problem: Ben wants to pay exactly 75¢. He has 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ and 50¢ coins. Which coins use the fewest coins?
steps: Take the largest coin that fits: 50¢. 75¢ - 50¢ = 25¢ is left.
The largest coin that fits 25¢ is 20¢. 25¢ - 20¢ = 5¢ is left.
Take a 5¢ coin. Nothing is left.

howto.title: How to pay an exact amount
steps: Take the largest coin that is not too much.
Subtract it from the amount. What is left?
Repeat with what is left. Stop at 0.

try.text: Pay exactly 80¢ with 3 coins. Use 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ or 50¢ coins. Write the coins. {b}¢ + {b}¢ + {b}¢

items.text: Count the money. Write the total. {b}¢
items.explanation: 50¢ and 10¢ make 60¢. Another 10¢ makes 70¢.

items.text: Count the money. Write the total. $ {b}
Fill in how many coins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 50¢ can be changed for {b} coins of 10¢.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 20¢ can be changed for {b} coins of 5¢.

parts.label: c
parts.text: $1 can be changed for {b} coins of 20¢.

parts.label: d
parts.text: $1 can be changed for {b} coins of 50¢.

items.explanation: (a) 10¢ five times is 50¢. (b) 5¢ four times is 20¢. (c) $1 is worth 100¢, and 20¢ five times is 100¢. (d) 50¢ and 50¢ make 100¢, which is $1.

items.text: Pay exactly with 2 coins. Use 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ or 50¢ coins. Write the 2 coins.
items.explanation: (a) 20¢ + 5¢ = 25¢. (b) 50¢ + 10¢ = 60¢. (c) 20¢ + 10¢ = 30¢. Try the largest coin that fits first.

items.text: Two of me make 40¢. Which coin am I?   {circ:5¢|10¢|20¢|50¢}
items.explanation: 20¢ + 20¢ = 40¢. Two 10¢ coins make 20¢. Two 50¢ coins make 100¢.

items.text: Look at the tags.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rubber and a pencil cost {b}¢ altogether.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which costs more, the ruler or the glue?   {circ:ruler|glue}

parts.label: c
parts.text: The ruler costs {b}¢ more than the rubber.

items.explanation: (a) 15¢ + 25¢ = 40¢. (b) 45¢ is more than 30¢, so the ruler costs more. (c) 45¢ - 15¢ = 30¢.

items.text: Ben pays 50¢ for a 30¢ sticker. How much change does he get? {b}¢
items.explanation: Change is what is left: 50¢ - 30¢ = 20¢. Count on to check: 30¢ and 20¢ more make 50¢.

items.text: Ali buys 2 toys for exactly $12. Which 2 toys? Circle them.
items.explanation: $4 + $8 = $12. Check the others: $7 + $4 = $11, $7 + $8 = $15 and $11 + $4 = $15, so no other pair makes $12.

items.text: Lily has $8. A book costs $13. How much more does she need? $ {b}
items.explanation: She needs the difference: $13 - $8 = $5. Count on: $8 and $5 more make $13.

items.text: Look at the 2 purses.
Mei buys exactly 2 toys for $15. There are 2 ways.
items.explanation: $6 + $9 = $15 and $7 + $8 = $15. The Drum needs $3 more, and no toy costs $3.

items.text: Circle True or False.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two 20¢ coins and one 10¢ coin make 50¢.   {circ:True|False}

parts.label: c
parts.text: A $1 coin is worth ten 10¢ coins.   {circ:True|False}

items.explanation: (a) 20 + 20 + 10 = 50: True. (b) three 10¢ coins make 30¢: False. (c) ten 10¢ coins make 100¢, which is $1: True. (d) four 5¢ coins make 20¢: False.

items.text: Pay with the fewest coins. Use 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ or 50¢ coins.
items.explanation: (a) 20¢ + 20¢ = 40¢. (b) 50¢ + 20¢ + 20¢ = 90¢. Start with the largest coin each time.

items.text: Circle the coins that pay exactly 65¢.
items.explanation: 50¢ + 10¢ + 5¢ = 65¢. Taking a 20¢ coin first leaves 45¢, which these coins cannot make.

items.text: Make 65¢ with exactly 4 coins. Use 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ or 50¢ coins. Find every set.
items.hint: Is a 50¢ coin in every set? Try with it, then without.
items.explanation: With 50¢, 15¢ is left, made by 5¢ + 5¢ + 5¢. Without 50¢, try 20¢ + 20¢ + 20¢ = 60¢, then 5¢ makes 65¢. A 10¢ coin makes no more sets.

items.text: Siti has 7 coins. They are 5¢ coins and 10¢ coins. Together they are worth 50¢.
items.hint: Guess how many are 5¢ coins. Does the total match?
items.explanation: Try 4 coins of 5¢ and 3 coins of 10¢. 4 x 5¢ = 20¢ and 3 x 10¢ = 30¢. 20¢ + 30¢ = 50¢, and 4 + 3 = 7 coins.

items.text: Make 40¢ with only 20¢ and 10¢ coins. Write every way in the table. Each row is one way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ways in the table.

answer.text: 2 coins of 20¢ and 0 of 10¢;  1 and 2;  0 and 4

items.explanation: Start with the most 20¢ coins. Two 20¢ coins make 40¢. One 20¢ and two 10¢ coins make 40¢. No 20¢ needs four 10¢ coins. That is 3 ways.
items.hint: Start with the most 20¢ coins you can use.

items.text: Friends share money equally.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Siti and Wei share 50¢. They have only 20¢ and 10¢ coins. Can each child get the same amount?   {circ:Yes|No}

items.hint: What is half of 50¢? Can those coins make it?
items.explanation: (a) 40¢ + 40¢ = 80¢. (b) 20¢ four times is 80¢. (c) Each child would get 25¢. Coins of 20¢ and 10¢ only make 10¢, 20¢, 30¢ and so on, never 25¢.

items.text: Wei pays with a $50 note for a bag and a hat. The hat costs $18. He gets $12 change.
items.hint: How much money did Wei really spend?
items.explanation: He spends $50 - $12 = $38 altogether. The bag costs the rest: $38 - $18 = $20. Check: $20 + $18 = $38 and $50 - $38 = $12.

items.text: Ali pays exactly $38. He has $1 coins and $2, $5 and $10 notes. He uses the fewest notes and coins.
items.hint: Start with the largest note that fits. What is left?
items.explanation: Three $10 notes make $30. $8 is left: $5 + $2 + $1. That is 3 + 3 = 6 pieces. Four $10 notes are too much, and no 5 pieces make $38.

items.text: Count the money. Write the total. {b}¢
Pay exactly 70¢ with 3 coins. {b}¢ + {b}¢ + {b}¢
items.explanation: 50¢ + 10¢ + 10¢ = 70¢. Without a 50¢ coin, 3 coins make 60¢ at most.

items.text: Ravi has 90¢. A drink costs 65¢. How much is left? {b}¢
items.explanation: 90¢ - 65¢ = 25¢. Count on: 65¢ and 25¢ more make 90¢.

items.text: Which is more money?   {circ:85¢|$1}
items.explanation: A $1 coin is worth 100¢. 100¢ is more than 85¢, so $1 is more.
